mcqs.question: A system starts slowing down under a simulated 10x traffic load. What's the strongest first move?
options: Add more app servers immediately, since app servers are the cheapest thing to add
Identify which layer actually saturates first, then scale that specific layer
Rewrite the system in a different architecture before scaling anything
Vertically scale the database preemptively without checking its current utilization
mcqs.explanation: The skeleton for this question is diagnose-then-fix: find the layer that's actually out of capacity before spending effort scaling anything. Adding app servers or resizing the database blind assumes an answer you haven't checked, and a rewrite is a massive overreaction to a capacity problem.

mcqs.question: Why can't you just add app servers behind the load balancer to handle 10x traffic if those servers hold session data in local memory?
options: Local session data means the load balancer can't route a user's next request to any node interchangeably, breaking horizontal scaling's core assumption
Reading from local memory is inherently slower than reading from a database
Load balancers can only connect to a fixed maximum number of servers
Session data has no effect on how the app tier scales
mcqs.explanation: Horizontal scaling assumes any node can serve any request. Local in-memory session state pins a user to one specific server, so adding nodes doesn't add usable capacity for that user's traffic. There's no such load-balancer connection cap, and local memory is normally faster, not slower.

mcqs.question: Horizontal scaling gives a near-unlimited capacity ceiling. What does it trade away compared to a single scaled-up box?
options: Nothing — horizontal scaling is strictly better in every dimension
It always costs more per unit of capacity than vertical scaling
Consistency and coordination simplicity — replicas and caches can now disagree, and requests need routing logic a single box never needed
The ability to handle further traffic growth at all
mcqs.explanation: Horizontal scaling buys near-unlimited capacity at the cost of coordination: multiple copies of state can drift, and you need routing/retry logic a single machine never required. It isn't strictly better in every way, isn't inherently more expensive per unit, and clearly doesn't cap growth — the opposite is true.

mcqs.question: App servers sit at 20% CPU but response times are climbing under 10x simulated load, and the database is at 95% CPU. What should you scale?
options: The app tier, since more servers always help under load
The load balancer, since it's the entry point for all requests
Vertically scale the app servers to a larger instance type
The database tier — it's the layer that's actually saturated; add read replicas or shard writes
mcqs.explanation: The app tier has plenty of headroom (20% CPU), so adding or resizing app servers won't move the needle — the database at 95% CPU is the real ceiling. The load balancer isn't indicated as saturated here either.
